newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House censures Mexico despite warnings.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House censures Mexico despite warnings.

text.p: The U.S. House of Representatives voted on Thursday to censure Mexico over its anti-drug efforts despite warnings that the action could spark a political backlash in Mexico.

The legislation would overturn President Bill Clinton's "certification" that Mexico is an ally in the fight against drugs unless he reports within 90 days that Mexico has made substantial progress in improving its performance.

But the legislation faces an uncertain future. In the Senate key members are backing away from a full-fledged confrontation with Mexico on its failure to stem a vast tide of drugs flowing across its long border.
Clinton stopped short of threatening to veto the measure, but criticised the vote, saying it was "the wrong way to protect the interests of the American people."

"I will continue to work with Congress to ensure that legislation that would undermine progress we have made with Mexico does not become law," he said in a statement from Florida, where he was travelling.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright called the vote "unwise and self-defeating," saying it would diminish the chance of making more progress.

"Decertification would damage our broader interests as well. It would shake financial confidence in Mexico and undermine the economic recovery we have done so much to promote," Albright said in a written statement.
If Clinton were to veto the congressional resolution it would take a two-thirds majority vote to override him.
Final House approval of the measure was by a vote of 251-175, less than the two-thirds needed to defy Clinton.

The resolution softens the blow to Mexico by waiving the economic sanctions that normally would result from such "decertification." It requires Clinton to report to Congress that he has obtained "reliable assurances of substantial progress" toward several objectives within 90 days.

They include allowing U.S. law enforcement officers in Mexico to carry arms -- something Mexico has refused to do, measures to eliminate official corruption, progress on extraditing Mexican drug traffickers to the United States and progress toward allowing U.S. vessels to stop and hold drug traffickers pursued into Mexican waters.

The congressional furore over Mexico's anti-drug efforts erupted last month when Mexico jailed its top drug-war official, Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo, on charges he was in the pay of a Mexican drug lord.

His arrest was announced on Feb. 18 as Clinton was weighing whether to re-certify Mexico as an anti-drug ally, which he did. Congressional critics said the arrest showed drug traffickers had penetrated Mexico's government.

But the Clinton administration insists Mexico has improved its anti-drug performance. It warns that overturning the president's Feb. 28 certification would undermine Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo's ability to make progress on drug control, with dire political and economic risks.

The administration also has warned that censure could lead to a loss of investor confidence in Mexico. Washington had to step in with billions in financial aid to its southern neighbour in early 1995 after investors lost confidence in Mexico and there was a run on the peso.
In Mexico City, the government blasted the House vote, calling it unacceptable, harmful to U.S.-Mexican relations and helpful only to drug traffickers.

"The resolution of the House of Representatives sends a wrong signal to Mexico and the world. The resolution damages international cooperation in the fight against drugs and benefits our common enemy: drug trafficking," the Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
